: Written by Wú Zhīqīng of the Ming Dynasty.
: The southern branch of Nánshān outside the city
: Extends from Hòucháo on Fènghuángshān up to Fēngshuǐ Cave and down to Gènshān
: Méizhú Hermitage
: The upper, middle, and lower sections each occupy one part, located in the area of Wànsōng Ridge, with secluded and narrow paths, high enough to overlook the river.
: Bōrě Temple
: Located to the left of the upper Méizhú path, formerly abandoned. In the Jiǎwǔ year of the Wànlì reign (1594), the monk Zhēnchéng Dìngchún rebuilt it, and there is a common ossuary pagoda.
: Bàoxiān Hermitage

: Located on Kǒngjiāshān. In the Jǐhài year of the Wànlì reign (1599), the monk Pǔmíng built it. Liú Hóngmó, magistrate of Rénhé County, initiated the project, and Fán Liángshū wrote a stele inscription, with the plaque "Zhuóxī Qīngsōng".

: Fán Liángshū's "Record of Bàoxiān Hermitage on Fènghuángshān": Fènghuángshān is a gathering place and divine marsh. On the north side of the mountain, Wànsōng Academy was originally the site of Bào'ēn Monastery. During the Hóngzhì reign (1488-1505), the Assistant Administrator, Duke Zhōu, destroyed the temple and built the academy to worship the former teacher Confucius, accompanied by the Four Sages, and ordered the descendants of the Kǒng family to guard it for generations, calling it Kǒngjiāshān. The mountain roads are lined with giant pines, lush and dense. From Wànsōng Lane, winding inwards, there is a small temple called Bàoxiān. In the Jǐhài year of the Wànlì reign (1599), the Venerable Pǔmíng came from Kuānglú and settled on this mountain. Liú Hóngmó, from my hometown, served as the magistrate of this county. The villagers, led by Jīn Gōng, Director of the State of Jiēzhōu, and Kǒng Gōng Chéngshì, requested the restoration of the hermitage. The hermitage is surrounded by mountains. To the left, it borders the lake; to the right, it embraces the river. It arches towards the city gates and leans against Bāpán, fully capturing the secluded beauty of this mountain. Behind the mountain, there are three ancient pine trees, swaying and leaning, with the potential to soar through the clouds. They reflect the sunlight of the county and city. After Pǔmíng's death, his disciple Shùshèng was able to maintain his legacy. Shùshèng is also from my hometown. The Buddhist teachings he follows were moved from Lúshān. Every year, patrons from Xījiāng provide rice for the "I-pú" offerings. They only drink the mountain spring water, which flows from the cracks in the rocks, enough to fill tea bowls. The monks all take refuge in the Venerable Shèng, rinsing their mouths with the wind, swallowing the moon, and chanting incessantly. Their disciples are respectful. I have observed that the monasteries in Húlín that are located in the lake and mountains are invariably burdened by the lake and mountains. The "Cong Yun Xiang Ge" pavilion is decorated with red jade and blue gems, and the clear stream bamboo forest is mixed with gold and emerald. The central harmony is disrupted. The sounds of the market are noisy, the dust of carriages rises like fog, singing and dancing are mixed together, and cups and goblets are intertwined, turning the pure land into a fiery house, which is truly regrettable. Only this mountain is far removed from the city, and fortunately, it is not inhabited by people. The hermitage sits among tall pines and slender bamboos, with a white cloud covering a valley and a clear stream flowing through it. The fragrance of Utpala flowers and the flourishing Bodhi trees suggest a pure and peaceful place. The Venerable Shèng and the monks leisurely stroll through the Shuangshu Forest, translating and expounding the Three Vehicles. Only the echoes in the mountains and valleys are heard. The Venerable asked me for a word to protect the spirit of the mountain. If this mountain has a spirit, there will surely be offerings and protectors in the future, just like Duke Liú and me, whose combined efforts, whether sooner or later, have been in harmony, so that even if the Buddhist monastery and the Kǒng Forest coexist, it is acceptable.
: Bàoguó Temple

: Located at the foot of Fènghuángshān, it is the site of the Jiànggǒng Hall of the Southern Song Dynasty. There is a gingko tree with fruit but without a heart at the corner of the hall. Yáng Zǎi's poem "Remembering the Past in Qiantang" says, "The ten-thousand-year pearl tree sheds autumn frost," probably referring to this. In the eleventh year of the Zhìyuán reign (1274), it was granted the name "Chánzōng Dà Bàoguó Temple." Chán Master Miàojì founded the temple. In the sixth year of the Yányòu reign (1319), it was destroyed by fire. The monk Dàxīn rebuilt it. It was destroyed by war at the end of the Yuan Dynasty. In the twenty-fourth year of the Hóngwǔ reign (1391), it was established as a "Conglin" monastery. In the Bǐngwǔ year of the Wànlì reign (1606), the monk Hǎiyīn renovated it. The old Mahavira Hall, Great Compassion Pavilion, Bìwú Pavilion, and Wǔfèng Pavilion were all Song Dynasty structures, but they were abandoned during the Yuan Dynasty. Of the five temples that were once the Southern Song imperial palace, only this one remains.
: Fàntiān Lecture Temple

: Built by the King of Wúyuè during the Qiándé reign (963-968) of the Song Dynasty, originally named "Nán Tǎ." It was renamed with its current name during the Zhìpíng reign (1064-1067). Destroyed during the Yuántǒng reign (1333-1335) of the Yuan Dynasty, it was rebuilt in the fifteenth year of the Yǒnglè reign (1417). There are two wells: the "Spiritual Eel Well" and the "Golden Well," and a stone pagoda, both five zhang tall, placed on the left and right of the gate. Previously, there was a Spiritual Eel Well on Mount Āyùwáng in Sìmíng. The King of Wúyuè welcomed the relics of Ashoka and enshrined them in Fàntiān Temple. An eel suddenly appeared when the well was dug in the south corridor. The temple regarded Sū Dōngpō as its "gālán" deity. The two monks Zànníng and Yùcénshān have records of this.

: Wáng Zàijìn's "Stele Inscription on Rebuilding Fàntiān Temple and Constructing the Guānyīn Pavilion": Hángzhōu has Fènghuángshān. Before the Tang Dynasty, it was Jiànzhōu, and Wúyuè established its state here. During the Southern Song Dynasty, the mountain was used as an imperial retreat. The mountain resembles a phoenix in flight, with its two wings spreading out. To the left, it borders the lake; to the right, it brushes the river. The clear waters flow back and forth, reflecting the light. The eastern foot of the mountain encircles the Song Dynasty capital's palace, lush and verdant, with beautiful and auspicious aura. Passing through Fèngshān Gate, turning south, then south again, and then west, one reaches Fàntiān Lecture Temple, which was built by the King of Wúyuè in the third year of the Qiándé reign (965). It was initially named Nán Tǎ and renamed with its current name during the Zhìpíng reign. It was destroyed during the Yuántǒng reign of the Yuan Dynasty and rebuilt in the fifteenth year of the Yǒnglè reign. Over the years, it had become dilapidated. In the Jiǎzǐ year of the Jiājìng reign (1564), the monk Chéngshān built the Buddha Hall. In the Jiǎchén year of the Wànlì reign (1604), Rénliáng built the Heavenly King Hall. In the Rénzǐ year of the Wànlì reign (1612), Lái Lún raised funds from local gentry, including the Imperial Secretary Hóng and the Minister Huáng, to jointly build the Guānyīn Pavilion, thus renovating the ancient Fàntiān Temple. Furthermore, a water pond and spring cellar were excavated and named "Xuánjìng," making the old ruins of Nán Tǎ once again a scenic attraction. From the Qiándé reign of the Song Dynasty to the present, 650 years have passed. The temple has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, but it has remained unchanged from the original legal structure of the Qiándé reign. The Buddhist temple and the rivers, lakes, and mountains will be forever established. Looking back at the Héníng Hall, the Xiángxī Hall, the Jíyīng Hall, the Chóngdé Hall, the Míngtáng, and the suburban sacrifices, the soaring and supportive structures have been transformed into green grass and blue sedge. The gold-covered and iron-clad structures have become thorny shrubs. The bronze camels, pavilions, gardens, and parks have been trampled into broken pottery and dirty corners. After the two rivers have cleared and the skies have cleared, the smoke from ten thousand households appears and disappears, gathers and scatters. The colors in the sky are all empty, but the most excellent monastery's Dharmakaya is not illusory. The three wheels always depend on the abode of non-abiding. The great undertaking of emperors is both existent and non-existent. Although it is overwhelming for a lifetime, it ultimately returns to nothing. The pure affinity of the empty gate is both non-existent and existent. The rise and fall follow each other and still return to existence. Existence returns to non-existence, which is the cycle of destiny. Non-existence returns to existence, relying on the immortal human heart. If the human heart is always there, then the Buddha-dharma is as present. The Buddha takes non-form as its essence, non-abiding as its principle, and wonderful existence as its function. The three paths and the Dharma realms gather together, and all the heavens protect and eliminate kalpic disasters. The Buddha speaks of endless dharma; I wish that all people would form endless connections. Wúyuè, Song, and Yuan are but a fleeting moment in the eyes of the world. The Lotus Sutra is fulfilled, and the Jìzhào Hall remains the same year after year. Please look at the Spiritual Eel Well and ask Mount Āyùwáng in Sìmíng. The rise and fall of the three realms change suddenly. Leaning and relying on each other, who is without and who is with? The bright moon on the mountaintop shines on people coming and going every night, unlike the desolate and cold imperial retreat of the Song Dynasty. Only Fàntiān remains unchanged today. The titles of the dignitaries are all there. I put my palms together and report to all the heavens. This is the inscription.

: Monk Shǒuchuán's poem: "The setting sun, cold cicadas chirp, I return alone to the temple under the trees. The brushwood gate is not yet closed at night; a sliver of moon follows my footsteps. I only hear the sound of dogs barking, then disappearing into the green vines."

: Sū Zǐzhān's reply poem: "I only hear the bell outside the mist, but I cannot see the temple in the mist. The recluse's journey is not yet finished; the grass and dew wet his straw sandals. Only the moon on the mountain should shine on those coming and going every night."

: "Poem on Visiting Jìzhào Hall at South Pagoda Temple during the Cold Food Festival": "The bells and drums south of the city contend for freshness, truly for washing away the miasma of exile. All are guests in the Hall of Mirroring Emptiness; who is the person in the mirror of silent illumination? The red blossoms return, the wind startles the dawn; green leaves become shade, the rain washes spring. Remember to celebrate the Cold Food Festival next year; the apricot blossoms were once neighbors with this old man."
: Qīyún Hermitage

: From Fàntiān, one resides in the mountains and follows the path upwards. Tall trees and dense bamboo surround the area, offering a glimpse of the river's waves. It is a secluded and leisurely place to practice Zen. Guàn Suānzhāi lived in seclusion here. Guàn's father, the Duke of the State of Chǔ, Guàn Jìgé Yùshí, therefore took Guàn as his surname and was called Suānzhāi. At the age of twelve or thirteen, he had extraordinary strength. He ordered strong men to drive three vicious horses at high speed. He stood with a spear, waiting for the horses to pass, crossed over two, and straddled three. The spear moved with the wind, and the onlookers retreated. He could also draw a strong bow to shoot and hunt fierce beasts, ascending and descending steep slopes as if flying. As he grew older, he devoted himself to reading books, and his eyes moved rapidly through the five classics. The lower hermitage was where he cultivated and stored his books. To the west, one can reach Lónghuá Temple.
: Shèngguǒ Chán Temple

: Shèngguǒ Chán Temple: Built by Chán Master Wúzhuó Xǐ during the Qiánníng period (894-898) of the Tang Dynasty. The King of Wúyuè carved images of Amitābha, Guānyīn, Daśamahāsthāmaprāpta, the Three Buddhas, and the Eighteen Arhats on the stone walls. At the beginning of the Qìnglì period (1041-1048) of the Song Dynasty, the prefect Zhèng Jiǎn requested the name "Chóngshèng Temple." Destroyed during the Zhìzhèng period (1341-1368), it was rebuilt by Guàn Chū Jìnggōng at the beginning of the Hóngwǔ reign (1368-1398), as recorded by Miáo Zhōng. Destroyed during the Yǒnglè period (1403-1424), it was rebuilt by the monk Zhèngyīn in the Wùwǔ year of the Jiājìng reign (1558). At the temple gate, there is a scenic view of rivers and mountains, inscribed by Jiǎng Gōng Huī, and the plaque reads: "Enter the deep pine path to open a famous temple; ascend the cloud-capped peaks to see the great river." The mountain shape soars and dances like a phoenix; the river tide surges. The pine path winds around, and the stream babbles, truly a magnificent sight. Beside the hall is the General's Pool. The bell in the bell tower was originally a Song Dynasty Jǐngyáng artifact. During the Jiājìng period, Vice Minister Hú took it to cast into military weapons. It was recast in the Rénzǐ year (1552). The magistrate of Rénhé County, Fán Liángshū, has a record of the bell tower. Ascending to the top, there are the ruins of the Thousand Buddha Pavilion, above which is the Three Pine Peak, and to the side is the Chóngshèng Pagoda, said to be seven levels and over twenty zhang tall, built during the Jǐngyòu period (1034-1038) of the Song Dynasty. Below is the Liǔpǔ, with its green shade, no different from an official embankment. Xià Gūizhōu studied here, and his question was, "The lonely peak of Heaven whistles; the strokes of the pen fly and dance." It is now in Sōngtāo Pavilion. Jiè Pavilion was built by Zǔ Wúzé and is located at Zhongfeng Pavilion. Zhongfeng practiced Chan meditation here. The Z zhōngshí Pavilion has the two characters "Fèngshān" written by Emperor Gāozōng of the Song Dynasty. The Golden Star Cave was written by the Prince of Luò of the Song Dynasty. The stone emits light on dark nights. There are also the Tōngmíng Cave, Flying Dragon Stone, Flying Cloud Stone, Ladder to Heaven, and Guānqī Stone. The Xǔsēng Spring's water is not enough to fill a handful, but it pours like a flood during a great drought. The Wòzuì Stone and the inscription on the Mist Cliff are as flat as a palm, with the Yangtze River as a pillow. There are also the Guīyún Cave and the Yuèyún Stone. Beside the stone is the Bamboo Garden, which is the Pagoda Garden of Chan Master Lǎn Gēng. The monks Hóng'ēn wrote the Tánluán Studio, and Wú Zhīqīng wrote the Chéngyī Pavilion, with the plaque reading: "Sparse paths curve and hide strange stones; purple vines deeply protect and absorb the heavenly flowers." It is said that the bamboo and stones are more beautiful together. Ascending the steps, one reaches the Moon Cliff. The peaks are sharply cut, with a gap like a mirror. The Mid-Autumn Midnight reflects each other like a perfect match. Many of the inscriptions and poems are moss-covered. The prostrate stone is like a tiger. The Great Vice Minister, Méilín Hú Gōng, viewed the sea and set off beacon fires here, and there is still a "Leaving Thoughts Stele" to this day. At the very top is the Imperial Drill Ground, where the Palace Commander's office of the Song Dynasty trained the imperial guards. The stone bamboo shoots are lined up, named "Pái Yá Shí," also called "Duì Shí." It is said that Emperor Xiàozōng ascended to the top during the Song Dynasty to review the river, wielding an iron staff weighing sixty catties, ascending and descending as if flying, to demonstrate martial prowess. It is also called the Women's Drill Ground. From here, the rivers and lakes are all within reach, and the red cliffs stand opposite each other. The line of the sea gate is fully visible.

: Tang Dynasty Monk Chǔmò's Poem: "The road ascends from Zhongfeng Peak, winding through vines. Reaching the river, the land of Wu ends, and across the bank are the mountains of Yue. Ancient trees cluster with green mist, and the distant sky is immersed in white waves. Below, the city walls are near, and bells and chimes mix with singing and music."

: Wáng Jièfǔ's poem: "Climbing high, I see mountains and water, my body in the center of the water. Looking down at the buildings, there are only many blue trees. Floating clouds connect to the sea's breath, and the setting sun stirs the lake's light. Occasionally sitting and playing the flute, the remaining sound enters Fuyang."

: Sū Zǐzhān's poem "Climbing Jiè Pavilion to bid farewell to Yáng Jié Cìgōng": "The bamboo sedan chair goes west, exiting the mountain gate, happy to seek a fairy village with my friend. The red and blue colors flicker on the Wind Bamboo Ridge, and the jade pendants echo in the empty Peach Blossom Spring. Yesterday morning, I wanted to climb, but the waxed clogs were useless; black clouds and white rain poured like a basin. This morning, the accumulated fog rolls away for a thousand miles; why fear touching the heat and developing sick roots? The ascetic at home, the non-doing one, has long been brothers with the blue mountains. At the end of the lonely peak, what else is there? West Lake mirrors the sky, and the river wipes the earth. Reaching the high point, I wave my hand to thank you; stay well, may the clear wind spread your words through ten thousand valleys. The wind returns the echo; listen to it, my friend. I also will follow your carriage everywhere."

: Yuán, the Dharma Master's poems and preface: "Shèngguǒ, a famous temple, faces each other, and the high pavilions and empty lofts fully capture the scenic beauty of the rivers and mountains. Inspired by Xie Xuancheng's line, 'Recognizing the returning boat at the edge of the sky, distinguishing the river trees in the clouds,' which is quite similar to this scene, I used it as a rhyme to compose ten poems and send them to Master Yù, a enlightened scholar of Shèngguǒ. Although it is insufficient to express elegance, I hope to convey the heart of mutual longing. * The color of the river is infinitely distant, vaguely connected to the distant sky. Returning sails carry the setting sun, and departing birds pierce the cold mist. Different scenic views are observed, and distant thoughts become this chapter. * The pavilions soar high, unevenly reaching the edge of the clouds. The morning light is fresh from the high windows, and the evening scenery has remaining rosy clouds. Few creatures move, and meditation removes the world's dust. * Cold and indifferent, difficult to group with, the secluded interest is only known by me. High emotions look down on the Milky Way, and pure talks moisten gold and stone. I do not learn from the floating world's people, who rush for fame and compete for carvings and decorations. * Only in stillness are a hundred worries forgotten. Opening the pavilion, all phenomena return to emptiness. The river answers the night bell, and the high peaks retain the remaining radiance. The secluded steps cut off worldly traces, and the lonely clouds rely on themselves. * Looking at evil is like touching hot water, and touching things is like an empty boat. Others cannot know, I know this path is what I seek. I miss you when sitting alone, as the setting sun falls below the dangerous building. * The towering high mountain is on the side, and touching the rocks produces patches of clouds, naturally bringing the expectation of heavy rain. I do not group with worldly scholars, but vaguely travel in the void, thinking of you many times in the face of this. * Who will be close to the high achievements? I live in seclusion among the white clouds. The idle steps spit out blue moss, and ancient trees produce a clear wind. I will often discuss and train the Western Buddhist poems to enlighten the ignorant. * Quiet and restless each have their preferences; how can right and wrong be distinguished? Fame and profit are like my enemies. If clouds and springs are pulled and pulled, I can cut the fragrant vegetation in the quiet deep forest. * The peaks tower with dangerous blue, and their reflections sink into the empty river. The clear scenery produces a late sunny day, and the cold color fills the empty windows. Leisurely indulging in chanting and admiring can make my heart surrender. * The sea sun shines on the chanting pavilion, and the river wind moves the courtyard trees. This scene is a joy between emotions; who knows
